They were going to hurt themselves if they kept going. They were also losing time standing here debating it. Both things were true and neither of them helped. "David—" "Not yet." “Guys we have to GO—" Her beam swung wildly, catching both of their faces in harsh slices of light. "Enough!" she barked, but it carried no decision, only the desperate need for one. Jake had been quiet through all of this. He'd stepped back from the door a minute ago, watching the group with an expression that had shifted from impatient to something more considered. "Hey." His voice cut through cleanly. "She wins if we keep doing this." Heads snapped towards him. "This." He gestured at the two of them at the door, at Dwight pulling at Orela, at the whole arrangement. "This is exactly what She wants. Us at each other’s throats. It doesn’t matter who’s right. If we keep arguing, we’re done.” David's hands had stilled on the crowbar. Leon had gone quiet. "We move," Jake said. "Together. Now." David and Leon stilled, leaning on the warped frame. Breathless, soaked, they staggered back, chests heaving. The tension in the air was palpable, both seeming to notice it properly for the first time. Leon looked to David. Waited. Another cough. A breath. David flexed lightly against the urge to argue. Jake was right, but that didn't make admitting defeat against a slab of rotten wood any easier. He gave the door an annoyed kick, water back-splashing against him in protest, then turned away from it. “Yeah. Ok. Let’s move.” Danny crouched low in a side room, the glow of his phone screen barely visible as he filmed their retreat, the survivors’ shapes bobbing in and out of the flashlight’s beam. From this angle, they looked less like people and more like fish in a tank, drifting through a hallway-turned-aquarium. Every splash, every stagger, every breathless mutter... it was art. He whispered into his mask, chuckling. "Swim faster, little minnows. Let’s see if you find the glass." Chapter 6 – Undertow The hallway had become a canal. Not dramatically — nothing in this building did anything dramatically anymore, preferring instead the slow patient version of every terrible thing. But somewhere between the front door and here the water had found the doorways and claimed them, rising until every opening along the hall was half-submerged, dark water lapping at the top of the frames with the quiet satisfaction of something that had been working toward this for a while. Orela kept the flashlight forward and her pace steady. The surface shimmered with movement, but the flashlight’s beam couldn’t break through it. Too murky. Too reflective. Orela swept the light ahead, but it bounced back off the water like a mirror. The floor beneath it was invisible, with nothing to mark where the hallway ended and the hazards began. Every step was a guess. Every footfall could find solid tile or find nothing, and there was no way to know which until weight was committed. “If you lose your footing in this,” Orela warned, “We won’t even see where you went down.” The water was too high now — licking mid-thigh — and the currents too deliberate. It tugged faintly, not downward, not outward. Away. From the walls. From the edges. Like the hallway itself was breathing inward. Jake squinted at the far end. “It’s pulling... do you feel that? It’s not just rising. It’s pulling...” Dwight pushed past him, pale and jittering, every nerve screaming at him not to stand still anymore. “One at a time. We stick to the wall.” They moved slowly. One of the basement stairwells appeared to their left — or rather, the top of its railing did, a few inches of metal standing above the waterline like a grave marker. Dwight glanced at it and quickly looked away. It shouldn’t have even been there in the first place, he noted mentally, not that it mattered. Nothing matched the layout he remembered anymore, and he would rather not think about it anyways. Orela led them forward, flashlight tucked high against her collarbone, her feet making slow steady slides across tile she couldn’t see. The beam caught glimpses of things beneath the surface — floating debris, a binder bloated with water, the shredded edge of a backpack. None of it sat still. The current nudged everything forward. The tiles were rough in places, near frictionless in others. She wished the light would break the surface better so at least she could tell what was in there. Her toes grazed a sharp edge, foot sliding suddenly into nothing, the tile vanishing beneath her. She jerked to a stop, hand flailing briefly for balance. Leon caught her arm on reflex, tugging her back from the edge. The light swung wildly, and the rest of the group froze in place behind her. Her flashlight beam skimmed across the water, catching the subtle fall where ripples slipped away into nothing. The hole into the basement was gone, swallowed entirely, leaving only a swirl of dark water that tugged on her legs expectantly. She stepped back quickly, steadying herself. “It’s open here,” she whispered. “Holy shit, I almost missed it completely.” David flinched lightly at the ripples. “Should have seen that coming. Let me guess. Swim across?” “We’re not backtracking,” Orela replied, voice firm. “I’m not going to risk wasting time checking classrooms to see if there’s a roundabout way past. This is... unpleasant, but more direct. If we keep a hand on the wall and take it slow, it’s not even that far across.” She didn’t wait for argument. Slid down into the water, slow and deliberate, then pushed off from the edge.
